Now, you indicated that Fazlic asked you to request of Commander Delic that he withdraw those units from Sarajevo, but when you look at that order and in particular in paragraph number 2, you will see there what purports to be an order, the 9th corps 1st brigade deputy commander to return to Sarajevo immediately in order to solve problems in the unit. Now, first of all you didn't ask Delic -- Commander Delic to order Ramiz Delalic to go back in person to Sarajevo, did you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you certainly didn't have any information of problems in the unit, the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Thank you. Those are the questions about that document. Now, finally, I think you indicated this before the break as to -- as to Commander Delic, but when you were present with Commander Delic, he acknowledged no connection whatsoever with this operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he said -- rather, what I remember in relation to that operation, he told me that he was familiar with the operation, but he was not familiar with all that many details, and that he would check it out and make the relevant decisions according to my requests. That more or less sums it up. He never mentioned issuing any orders and especially what would be the content of such an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I just want to remind you of something that you said in your statement to the investigators here and ask you to comment on it. This is a statement relatively recently of the 4th of March, 2004, and I've quoted one part of it to you already. At paragraph 24, you said this to the investigators: "Rasim Delic" -- I'm quoting now, so I'll go slowly. "Rasim Delic said that he knew very little or almost nothing about the operation, and I have the feeling that he did not know that Halilovic was down there."

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He tried to put it to me in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You didn't believe a word of it, did you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already mentioned that it would be illogical for him not to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was your reaction even before you'd seen that map which you've looked at today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, those are the questions on that topic. Now I want to return to some other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I'd ask, please, that the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will just have to forgive me here, Mr. Tirak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want everyone to remember that this is a paper-free court, and I would ask that the witness please be shown D270 -- sorry, D151. D151 is the exhibit number. This is a document that's already been tendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm going to show you now is a document that you may or may not have seen, but I'll ask you to comment upon it regardless. It's in evidence now. This is a letter from Enes Kovacevic addressed to -- personally to the commander of the 6th Corps and it's dated the 13th of September, 1993, in Jablanica. Do you have that document on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first of all, Enes Kovacevic was the commander of the 44th brigade, sometimes referred to as the Jablanica Brigade; is that correct. 44th mountain brigade I should say?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this document here, this appears to you to be a communication requesting information from the commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you see in this letter Kovacevic refers to him briefing the chief of the SVK, Supreme Command Staff, about the possibilities of certain combat operations and that thereafter a request was sent to the command of the 6th Corps for the reply -- for the supply of necessary material and technical equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that your role as Chief of Staff -- I'm stepping outside of this document for a moment. I just want to ask you this. Your role as Chief of Staff concerned, among other things, the provision of logistics. Can I ask you whether -- look, I won't ask you that yet. I'll ask you a question about logistics in a minute. I'll take you through the rest of the -- of the letter and then I'll ask you. Okay. Now, does it appear here that Kovacevic is saying that on the evening of the 11th of September, the corps commander, which is presumably Salko Gusic, informed me in person about -- in a telephone conversation about the activities of the 44th Mountain Brigade and promised the equipment that we requested. Do you observe that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph does Kovacevic say this: "We were expecting -- during 12th of September we were expecting the corps commander to come in order to work out the details for the next combat operations, but as we have so far not received anything concrete regarding the planned operation -- the planned combat operations nor the materiel support, we are asking you to inform us about the following." Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then do you see that Kovacevic then makes two further requests of -- of Salko Gusic, of the commander, concerning firstly the provision of equipment under number 1, but secondly, the question is asked "Is the 45th brigade going to conduct combat operations?" Do you see those two questions?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tirak, obviously your evidence here has clarified a number a things, and I think the main thing it's clarified is that you were -- you were not present obviously when this letter was received; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand you indicated in the past that you weren't aware of the involvement of the 6th Corps command in these combat operations. Would you agree with me -- with this, you have -- in fact, you have never seen this letter before today, have you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days earlier, the -- a few days ago, the Prosecution showed it to me by way of preparation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At the time when the combat operations were taking place, though, you didn't know about this letter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor show you any other documents concerning -- well, I'll ask you that in a minute. We'll come back to that. Now, turning to the substance of this -- of this document here, what you say is didn't know anything about these conversations between the commander of the 6th Corps and Enes Kovacevic, the commander of the 44th brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suppose the reason you didn't know anything about it is you were doing the best you could to fulfil your obligations in other parts of the 6th Corps zone of responsibility. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the -- it's entirely possible that on the 11th of September, you were either on your way to or already in the city of Visoko in order to speak to Commander Delic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It strikes me as possible based on the documents that you've shown me, but I must say this again, I can't remember the specific date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. It's -- no -- it's -- we understand it's many years ago. All right. Well, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown another document. This one is D150. It's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what's going to be shown to you is an order written by Mr. Zejnilagic who was the commander -- well, perhaps I could ask you this while we're waiting for that order to come up. Was the commander of the 317th Brigade, a man named Zejnilagic.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what we have -- what I'm putting to you here is a document that was tendered through another witness, but it's an order by Zejnilagic. What I want you to do is to focus on the preamble of that order. Do you see that this order by Zejnilagic is headed "Order to attack"? Do you see that heading?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And orders to attack are sometimes described as combat orders in your experience; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it's part of -- it's customary for commanders, when writing -- when issuing an order to attack to place -- I'll start that question again. It's customary for intermediate commanders when issuing an attack order to put in the preamble to the order the basis of their authority, in other words, how they come to be allowed to issue attack orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, here Mr. Zejnilagic relies on two orders. One is an order of the NGS, Chief of General Staff, which doesn't have a number or date attached to it, and also to a command of the commander of the 6th Corps which does have a number attached to it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason for putting that number on it -- on a document like this is to allow anyone who looks at -- at the document to find in the archives the other order by reference to the number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that the order of the 6th Corps -- sorry, the commander of the commander of the 6th Corps is given the number 01/1500/27 dated 11 September 1993. Does that appear to be the case in your Bosnian document?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time of the 11th of September, 1993, I understand you can't recall precisely where you were on a precise date, but you did not know about this order of the command -- this command of the commander of the 6th Corps back in September of 1993. That was not something you knew about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in any event, it was within your knowledge that the 317th Brigade was at least in theory supposed to be under the role of the 6th Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the moments that were much debated and also one of the reasons I went to Visoko to see Mr. Delic and speak to him. If you look at the number 3, formally speaking, you can see that this is within the composition of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, looking at that third paragraph, I don't want to deceive you about this but just so you understand what the situation is, Operations Group West was in the 3rd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there's one thing you must understand. We are talking about the circumstances that were there at the time. It happened a number of times, also before and after that the respective competencies or authorities were not really that clear. The situation on the ground was a lot more complicated than it seems when you look at the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, I think you would make the comment that the war looks nice and clean when you look at the documents, but the reality on the ground was a lot more confusing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But -- although -- acknowledging what you say to be right there, nevertheless it appears in -- on the face of this order here that Zejnilagic, the commander of the 317th Brigade, is acknowledging that he derives his authority to issue combat orders in part from a combat order of the 6th Corps commander; is that correct? Having regard to the introductory paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once again -- I'll withdraw that. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would the witness be shown another order. Now, this one is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another order which is relevant to these matters.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. There is a remark I'd like to make in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Feel free.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is highly unusual for a brigade commander to issue an order with two units involved that are actually not within his brigade. So, obviously, if we look at it today the way it looks this might be another one of those orders that were issued as an alibi throughout the war. It's just a remark, an observation that I'd like to make to show you that the documents don't always reflect the situation on the ground in a faithful light.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you have picked no fight with me on that topic, but I'll make comments about it in -- in the closing address. I'll just leave that for now. Thank you for that comment, however. Could I just ask now you have the chance to look at -- just -- sorry. Before that -- before that goes off, and in light of the comment you just made there, were you personally aware that any combat that took place in the Uzdol area or the areas described in that order after the 15th of September? In other words, are you personally able to say that this order was ever acted on by anyone?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I simply don't know, but based on my experience, it might easily have been the case, that the order was indeed not acted on. But I have to say this again, I simply don't know. I know at the time the 317th faced a great deal of difficulty in terms of their interhuman relations between the battalion -- the relations between the battalion and the brigade commander. And I have no idea whether they took any steps at all in that respect. I simply can't say one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could the witness please be shown -- it's -- Pardon me, I've got the Defence document numbers. Just excuse me, please. It's D149. That's the exhibit number, D149.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're going to be shown now is a combat report coming out of the Independent Prozor Battalion, and in particular from Mr. Enver Buza. And it's a relatively thorough and complete document, so I'll ask you to just -- to scan it quickly. Now, does this appear to be an undated combat report from the Independent Prozor Battalion? In fact, it's got a date when it was received at military security but the document itself may not have a date. But in any event, an undated report by -- from -- combat report to the 6th Corps command signed by or under the hand of Commander Enver Buza. Is that what it appears to be to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Enver Buza was indeed the commander at the time. I don't know whether this signature belongs to him and whether he was the one who actually produced this document. Probably so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. I won't -- I won't ask you to look at Mr. Buza's signature at this stage, but do you know notice that that report, that combat report to the commander -- to the command of the 6th Corps refers to an order number in the first line of the substantive text refers to an order number 01/1500-27 of 11 September 1993? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when I showed you the Zejnilagic order a minute ago that that also referred to that same combat order number which I read out at the time? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. It may be so. I didn't really pay close attention to that number. I suppose it's true, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, look, if I've misled you about that number the Prosecutor will be able to jump up and tell -- and tell us. I hope I've read it out to you accurately. In any event, it appears, doesn't it, that both Buza and Zejnilagic have conducted combat operations pursuant to that order with that number coming from the 6th Corps command of the 11th of September 1993? Does that appear accurate to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it looks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That much is certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you had the opportunity just to -- to look through that particular document, and in particular I'm interested in the last paragraph or so where -- where Enver Buza makes the comment: "By my estimate, about 65 Croatian soldiers and about 30 civilians, mostly armed, were liquidated during the operation. One should bear in mind that the Ustasha artillery was literally destroying the entire Uzdol sector the whole time." Could I just now -- I mean, you're entitled to read the whole thing because I don't want to surprise you with anything here. But that's the passage want to ask you about in a minute. Have you found that passage?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please go on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. Do you need -- well -- okay. Have you read that passage where it says "by my estimate about 65 Croatian soldiers and about 30" -- okay. Well, my question is: As Chief of Staff of the -- of the 6th Corps didn't somebody tell you about that pretty quickly when that information became available, or were you tied up somewhere else in the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much later when I heard what occurred over there, although not much time had gone by, I went there soon after, but I was familiar with the unit, and I asked them to give me whatever information the corps was in possession of at the time. Among other things, I remember this document very clearly. I read through it back then and, to put it mildly, I found it unbelievable that this unit could have eliminated so many soldiers, given the fact that I knew how poorly equipped the unit is, with no military experience whatsoever and made up entirely by local farmers. So, to sum it up, this report struck me as -- I'm not sure about the expression I should use. I think it exaggerated. I think Mr. Buza was being boastful, and he was trying to represent his military successes as much greater than they had been in actual fact. It was only much later --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that I found out that a crime had been committed over there. But if I may be allowed to say what I feel personally, I still find it difficult to believe that those peace-loving farmers could have done anything like that. To this day I have not been able to establish with certainty who it was. I suppose it's down to this Tribunal to determine that. My position remains what it used to be. It strikes me as unbelievable, which does not necessarily make it impossible, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But you certainly would never have foreseen the Prozor Battalion doing anything terrible like this, would you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw those people, I'm talking about my experience, I just couldn't believe it. That's just a very subjective perception, and of course it could change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I just want a document to be put on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I'm proposing to do now is to show the witness the front page, and it's really a signature matter now, so I've -- it's -- it's not the substance of the witness statement, it's just the signature on the first page of the witness statement of Bahrudin Fazlic, so I ask that be placed on the ELMO, please, so the witness can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm going to do now is show you -- on the screen it will come up at some point but you can probably look at it just as well from where it is. In any event, this is a signature of Mr. Fazlic, and I just ask you to look at that, please, and tell us, do you recognise that signature yourself as being the signature of Mr. Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. Last time I saw his signature was many years ago. I can't say with certain whether it is or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I won't ask you for certainty, but does that -- does that signature appear familiar to you as the signature of -- of Bahrudin Fazlic, a person with whom you worked quite closely in those months?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looks like it, although as I've already said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to seek to tender that front page just with that signature on it. What -- what we'll do is -- at the moment it's attached to a statement but what we'll do is to -- to detach it and offer it for tender. It's not currently upload. The purpose of doing that will be apparent in 60 seconds, I hope, so I'll offer it for tender now and I'll seek to justify it later, depending on what happens with the next document, frankly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 295.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage I would object to that. First of all, the within has been equivocal about the signature of the person it says it is and secondly, I can't see at this point the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll make our ruling after we hear the other evidence on this aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, my learned friend's quite right to raise the issue of relevance and its relevance or otherwise will be proved by the next document. Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I want to show you now is another document. This one is D152. Now, this document that's coming now is a combat order, and indeed it's a"V" combat order with the number on it which has -- which appeared in the Zejnilagic order and in the Buza combat reported. So I will just ask you to have a look at that first of all. Do you now have in front of you an order to attack dated at Dobro Polje on the 11th of September, 1993, and bearing that same number 01/1500-27? Just take a moment to read over that, and if you need to turn over the page, feel free. You will notice at the end it's signed by a sort of a -- a scrawl rather than anything that looks like a particular signature, and I'll ask you to comment on that as well, if I can.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the first question I have is that this document is in form an attack order, a combat order emanating from the 6th Corps command and directing the following units to go into battle in a particular way: The Prozor Independent Battalion, a unit of the 45th Mountain Brigade, battalions of the 317th Brigade, and platoons of the Sutjeska Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this -- this order has been authorised by somebody who signed in the top left-hand corner underneath the words Dobro Polje 11th of September, 1993. And I want to ask you when you look at that there, that appears to be the signature of Mr. Fazlic, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite illegible. Could be. You'd have to ask him, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're the one the Prosecutors have called here, Mr. Tirak, so I have to ask you. Is your position this: You can't say because it's just not a good enough quality signature?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've observed yourself that it appears quite illegible. If you look at the first letter, I'd be inclined to say, yes, it is his signature. He had this distinctive way of combining V and the F. Very particular, very peculiar. But I really can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it assist you to have that blown up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness have that section where the signature is enlarged on the screen, if possible? And if I could ask the Court Deputies to assist by showing everyone in the courtroom that section of the Bosnian version rather than the English one, which is in nice, typed words -- a signature. Your Honours, I make that demand very high-handedly. I don't know if that technically can be done. I believe it can, but I'm -- if it can be done. I'm sorry. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have an expanded version of that in front you now?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But it's difficult for me to say. I can't say yes and I can't say no. I can't commit myself categorically. I can neither deny it nor confirm. The first letters of the signature look very much like his, but then the line that follows looks a bit inarticulate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So all -- so is this an accurate way to put it: You'd say that the start -- that the start of that signature looks very similar to his distinctive signature style but the rest of it is just not able to be the subject of an opinion by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you. Now, let me ask you a question about this document generally. Those are the questions I've got about the signature, and that's -- Your Honours, that's the reason -- to answer my friend's objection. That's why -- that was the relevance of showing the other document with that signature on it, so that's why it's being done. Now, could I just ask you about the substance of this document. First of all, were you told yourself that Mr. Fazlic or indeed any other senior -- senior officer at the 6th Corps had issued this order on the 11th of September, 1993? And I mean, did you know that back at the time. I don't mean subsequently.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlic told me that based on the agreement reached at Jablanica that I've already mentioned, he had issued certain orders. I'm not sure if that particular remark was in relation to this order or something else, but he did state unequivocally that he had issued orders pursuant that agreement. Which specific orders, now this is something that you need to go and ask him not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as I said, unfortunately the Prosecution have put you in the witness box here so I have to ask you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry but I resisted last time. There is no need for this kind of commentary. It's just not relevant to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You could save a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours it's just really byplay with the witness when he makes a comment. My friend's right. It's not relevant. I'm not seeking to rely on my own comments. I can promise the Court that. Sometimes witnesses are treated in an uncivilised way and that sort of commentary just was an attempt to be civilised, but I understand what my friend says and I won't say anything like that in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, sorry about that Mr. Tirak. Very well. But at all events were you shown that document by the Prosecutor in proofing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you shown that other one that I -- you indicated that you were showed the letter from Kovacevic in proofing. Were you shown the Zejnilagic order in proofing with the Prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you shown the Buza order in proofing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you shown the Fazlic statement in proofing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from that Zejnilagic -- sorry pardon me. I withdraw that. Apart from the Kovacevic that you were shown in proofing, what other documents did the Prosecutor show you? You've indicated of course the supposed order of Delic of the 12th. So that's two documents. What else did they show you in this proofing session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I have also resisted in the past, but comments like supposed order of Delic when in fact that document was a Defence exhibit and in fact sought to be tendered by the Defence suggests to me that that kind of comment is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that Defence is entitled to ask what kind of documents the witness was shown during the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's not a problem, Your Honour. I'm just merely commenting on the comment by learned counsel with respect to the Delic order that it is a supposed order and in the past purported order, when in fact it is an exhibit they themselves tendered. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just bear in mind the objections from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I bear them in mind but I don't want anybody to be under any misapprehension about that. We did tender it, and it's always been our position that it's a supposed or purported order, and we're tendering it with the faults that we say it has. That's why, and I'm going to continue to refer to it in that way unless there is some substantive problem with doing so. Your Honours, I will proceed with the question, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the question to you is did they show you - sorry - did they show you any other documents apart from those two in the proofing sessions?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean whether the ones that you've shown me now had been shown to me? I've already said no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. No, I didn't -- yes -- no, you've already clarified that very well. But the question was, have they shown you any other documents?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was shown several documents but not these ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay what other documents were you shown in proofing. Perhaps I'll just stop you -- I'll stop you there for a moment. Perhaps I'll be a little more circumspect about it. Were you shown any other documents in proofing that related to the combat operations in Herzegovina? I don't want to know about irrelevant ones, Mr. Tirak, but just ones relating to the combat operations in Herzegovina late in August and through September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to those documents, I was shown two documents, the document from Mr. Kovacevic and the one from Mr. Delic and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, without saying what the other documents were, were they documents that related to you or were they documents that related to the case here?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shown documents relating to me, but I can, of course, answer those questions if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I mean I'm only going to ask them if they're relevant, frankly, if they're relevant to the case. Do those documents have anything to do with the 6th Corps' involvement in combat operations in Herzegovina in the months of August and September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just excuse me one moment, please. I'm sorry. I just want to consult with my learned colleague for a moment. Just hold on for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just checking the time there. Your Honours, when is the time for the break to be taken?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it now is the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just bearing in mind look it would be appropriate now I think as history shows it sometimes speeds up the final questions if we have a short break. So yes I would seek that the break be taken now if that's okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will take a 15 minutes' break, so we will resume at five minutes past six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks, Your Honour. Things will be quicker as a result of all of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I just ask you -- I was asking you about documents shown to you in the proofing session before the break. Now I just wish to ask you -- having considered the matter in the break, I ask you what are the other documents that you were shown in proofing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In conjunction with that operation, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've indicated that these matters related to you -- I think you indicated that some of the documents related to you personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks I just have one other matter to raise with you now before I finish. You've indicated that after you -- after you came back from Zenica, you went back to Fojnica with a the petrol tanker and you were there for a couple of days. Did you personally take part in -- in the combat operations against the HVO on the axis between Gornji Vakuf and -- and Vrdi in the week after you came back from -- from Visoko?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't quite understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I'll put the question better. When you came back from Visoko and Zenica, did you essentially resume your duties in the Fojnica-Vakuf area?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I returned from Zenica -- rather, from Fojnica, I returned to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get that place that you returned to, Mr. Tirak. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean after my meeting Mr. Delic, I went to Zenica, afterwards to Fojnica, and from Fojnica I returned to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately what date did you get to Konjic? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to have a look at one document here. This is already admitted into evidence. It's D159. And this is a letter, I think, emanating from the deputy commander of the Bosnian army standing in for Rasim Delic at the time, Stjepan Siber. And it's an inquiry and I just ask you to look --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Stjepan Siber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to forgive me bad pronunciation. I'm sorry about that. And would you just have a brief look at that and just tell us did you ever see that document -- or did you see that document in mid-September 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself had not seen it, but I know that when I got to the corps I was told that Mr. Siber had been asking for extra information. And not just him; they said that any number of people were looking for information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes just -- this might help us to get -- to fix a date as to when you came back to Konjic. You came to Konjic after this Siber letter had arrived there, I take it. Even though you didn't see it, you heard about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose, but let me stress once again don't ask me about the dates and times too much because I really can't tell you with any degree of precision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. It's just -- perhaps since the letter's dated the 16th, can you remember whether you arrived back at Konjic on the same day as this letter arriving or was it a couple of days later? What's the best memory you have of that? And I understand you can't be too precise, but do the best you can.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. To be honest, as far as I remember -- well, all this is somehow confused, and I even tended to think that was happening in the beginning of October. And it was only when I was shown some papers that I realised that it actually took place in September. So my memory seems to be failing me a little bit in this business. Perhaps consciously and unconsciously I'm trying to forget it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you for that. Could I just ask finally that the witness be shown a document now. This is an unrelated matter now, but this is an order and it's -- look, I apologise, Your Honours. That is a recently decided upon document. It hasn't been uploaded yet, and I apologise to all concerned. We'll just to do it with paper now, and could we distribute copies to the Prosecutors and ... I'm told that was only translated yesterday, Your Honour. I can say from my own experience that a decision to use it was taken at about lunchtime. What's going to be shown to you now in hard copy because it's not on the computer system yet, Mr. Tirak, is an order which you may or may not have seen. I just ask you to look at it and -- and read it and consider it. What you're going to be shown is an order -- sorry, not an order, a -- a piece of correspondence coming from Visoko from a IKM at Visoko, and referring to a proposal by the 6th Corps to regulate the status of a number of small units, and you'll see their name there, the Handzar Division, the Akrepi, and the Silver Fox units. As you read, I'll just point out the thing I'm interested in so that you know what my questions are about. You'll look at this -- you'll look there. You'll see that there's reference to an order of the SVK commander, and it's given a number, that's an order of Delic, of Rasim Delic, ordering some -- some of these small units to go and join the 4th Corps. And then another order issued by the SVK chief. He's not named there but it's obviously Sefer Halilovic, an order sent from the command post to the 44th Brigade, which directed the Handzar Division and Silver Fox to join Zuka's unit. And then at the bottom there's this comment: "Since neither of these orders was implemented, the 6th Corps command hereby requests on the basis of the said document that these units be ordered to disband." Now, I want to ask you firstly do you remember this order and have you seen it -- do you remember this -- this communication? Have you seen it before? And then whether you have or you haven't, I'll ask you to comment on the subject matter of it and what it says. So first of all, can I ask you were you familiar with that piece of correspondence at the time in November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is waiting I think that's MFI296.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In November 1993, I was on my way out of that corps, so I can't really say that I know of this letter, but I did know, because from the very start, from the setting up of the corps and afterwards, we've always had this problem and we kept referring to it all the time. We kept bringing it up. That is to say that in the area of responsibility of the 6th Corps, very often units cropped up that were not under our command and control and we kept stressing that that issue had to be resolved. And this is probably one in a series of letters that were being sent all over the place in order to try and finally sort this problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you indicate just from the markings on that document, did that pass through -- where did that originate, that document, and who did it go to?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- I mean, this document, the way it stands here, it comes from one of the administration offices, and it was sent to IKM Visoko, and basically it means to Mr. Delic. That's what I think at least, because when you say Visoko IKM, you mean that it's Mr. Delic, but maybe it's not. It's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I understand what you say is that you don't specifically recall this document. Do you remember Mr. Avdula Lakic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you can say this is a document coming out of the 6th Corps, and you can say that it relates to matters which were the subject of ongoing correspondence by the 6th Corps in an attempt to clean up the problems referred to in it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document does not come from the 6th Corps. We can tell. But it is a consequence of proposals coming from the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer that document for tender notwithstanding the witness hasn't seen it because of the way it's exchanged between -- between army units. So, yes, I offer that document. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I would object to that. The relevance primarily. I can't see the relevance to the case at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'm sorry. I'm happy to explain that my friend's right to ask me to justify it. I notice the objections about relevance and the issue of relevance really is, quite plain on the face of it, when you look in the middle of it here. The Prosecutors tendered some documents nearly the trial concerning the 4th Corps, and there was a chain of resubordination of minor units that were supposed to send the Zulfikar unit and other small units from the 6th Corps into the 4th Corps and then, ultimately, according to these orders - none ever which have been proved - into the -- to be subordinated to or -- sorry, to receive tasks from the IKM. Now, what the Defence has said is, well, these orders were never put into practice and this document here says and makes it quite clear neither of these orders was implemented. And it's a recognition by the army itself in November of 1993 that the orders by Delic on the 1st of September and Sefer Halilovic on the 2nd of September concerning resubordination of units were never implemented. It's directly relevant in that respect. It speaks for itself, frankly, and -- so that's the relevance of it and I seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Defence asked some questions to this witness concerning this document, and at the beginning of this document it says opinion on proposal by the 6th Corps. So there is some relevance to this witness. This document is admitted into the evidence. Of course, as for the weight the Bench attaches to it, we will deal with it at a later stage. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases. But the final questions I have really concerns the situation of choosing the troops from Sarajevo, and that's my last questions for you, Mr. Tirak. First of all, I understand what you've said about your opinions concerning the choosing of troops for offensive operations. As for the situation in the first week of September of 1993, I take it you were extremely busy trying to save the situation in Fojnica and do your job properly in Fojnica; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as to the 1st and 2nd glorious brigades who were part of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo, you can't comment, can you, as to whether they had any troops available as in the first week of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the situation at that particular moment in the 1st Corps, I can't really say much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I'm limiting my questions to this particular time which is the time when these troops were selected. As to the situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll just indicate for the Court's comfort, I think there's three minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tirak. My apologise. As to the situation in the 4th Brigade which was based at Hrasnica, in the first week of September of 1993, you don't know whether they had any troops to spare either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that as to the general state of affairs in the 1st Corps, and that brigade was a part of that corps, I couldn't give you any specific information about that because I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, I was going to go through unit by unit, but what you're telling me is that there's no point doing that, you just didn't really know about the specific situation with any of those units in the 1st Corps in that first week of September. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in that event, that's the end of my questions. Thank you for your patience in answering them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any redirect examination in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Might the witness be shown Defence D152. I think that is the document. Re-examined by Mr. Sachdeva:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, do you see that document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, given your evidence about -- given your evidence that you cannot confirm or deny that this document was signed by Mr. Fazlic, for the purpose of this question, assuming that it was signed by Mr. Fazlic, does this document change your view as to the involvement, the level of involvement of the 6th Corps in the operations to liberate Mostar, in terms of a command involvement?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether this document alone confirms or fails to confirm what I was told. It is a fact, though, that the 6th Corps command issued the relevant orders to the units within the 6th Corps' composition. However, based on this document alone, one can't really say whether they took part in the operation in its entirety. No one has ever shown me a document showing the 6th Corps issuing orders to units outside the 6th Corps that were in the area at the time. It was only to be expected that pursuant to any instructions that is they may or may not have received. I don't know myself, but that's what Mr. Fazlic told me. It was only to be expected, as I say, that based on the instructions they had received from the forward command post, the Supreme Command Staff, they would be issuing orders to units but units within the 6th Corps and not any other units. Based on that, one might be led to conclude that they did not command the entire operation but just a fragment of the operation and in as far as the units of the 6th Corps were involved. That is my position. That is how I see things, but it may be obvious that I know little about this operation after all as what others have told me and what I have pointed out myself on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, then: Counsel for the Defence asked you when you were over in Fojnica about the 6th Corps being involved in the operation to liberate Mostar. Now, I want you to be absolutely clear if you can. Irrespective of whether the situation was normal or abnormal, irrespective of that, if the 6th Corps had been involved in the operation to liberate Mostar, in other words, if it was running the operation to liberate Mostar know star, would you have known about it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry could I just intervene for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours that's asking for a speculative answer there. He's -- it's just not based on the concrete case and it doesn't arise directly out of the questions that I asked. It really was the case in evidence in chief as it emerged, and frankly I'll make this comment. As it changed in the witness's evidence that -- that the -- the Prosecution is relying on the fact that this witness didn't know things to establish that they weren't happening. That's really the way this evidence evolved. And that's no criticism of the witness, but that was what was said in evidence in chief. And my friend is entitled to identify a specific problem and he can clarify it, if there is anything that needs for clarified. But that there, it seems to me just to be an attempt to do re-evidence in chief once again, and I object to it. And it doesn't arise directly from a question of mine as Your Honours will see from the attempt to quote it as a question by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may put your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Might I just respond to that, if I may, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Counsel for the Defence has put -- firstly I should -- should have risen at the time, but mischaracterised my questions to the witness. My questions in evidence in chief were about the 6th Corps' involvement in terms of its command relationship with the operation to liberate Mostar. Counsel for the Defence alluded to my questions with respect to its participation in the involvement, participation in the operation to liberate Mostar, and, in fact, in answer to my question about the command relationship with the operation to liberate Mostar, Mr. Tirak said, "If the command of the 6th Corps had planned a large-scale operation like this, I would have been involved without a shadow of a doubt." Now I'm simply trying to get clarification from the witness as to whether, in his answers to the Defence counsel in cross-examination, he is talking about 6th Corps being involved running the operation, planning the operation, or simply participating in the operation. And to me that's a very essential distinction in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is an essential distinction. And why didn't they ask it in evidence in chief, if that's the case. I mean, that distinction there is central, but, frankly, in my submission that's -- look, in any event, frankly, I think it should be permitted to ask the question so I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but you may ask some questions to clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, you've told the Court that three units of the 6th Corps were -- were involved in the operation to liberate Mostar. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's not accurate he's told the Court that Mr. Fazlic has told him some things about it. He hasn't told the Court anything like that. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. I'm thankful to my friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the court that Mr. Fazlic had told you that Mr. Halilovic had asked for three units of the 6th Corps to be involved in the operation to liberate Mostar. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is something that Mr. Fazlic told me. I believe I've said that this a number of times already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Fazlic tell you or did you learn or do you have knowledge of whether the 6th Corps ran the operation to liberate Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to that question. This witness has been called really to relay what Fazlic told him. I've made my complaints about that and I'm not going to repeat them. But what he thinks what the situation might have been is absolutely irrelevant. He wasn't there he doesn't pretend he was there. So it's just -- it's not just -- it's totally irrelevant to ask this question, what his view about it is, and I object to that question and similar ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I respectfully disagree. I'm not asking what the witness thinks. I'm asking what he knew and what he was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe this Bench has already allowed you to make some clarification on that issue. The question is how do you put your question in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask the question another way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, as Chief of Staff of the 6th Corps and taking into account your evidence that you were in Vakuf and Fojnica at the time, my question is this: If the 6th Corps was running the operation to liberate Mostar, would you as the Chief of Staff have known about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, again I object. It's the same question again. It's speculative. It's got all the other faults. I object to it again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I'm not understanding something, but I cannot see how this is speculative. Simply because -- well, I will resist from making submissions that may prejudice an answer by the witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, given it's a new question, at this stage we will allow the witness to answer the question, and the Defence will have the opportunity to cross on that issue if they believe it is necessary. Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I've answered this question already, loud and clear. I said it loud and clear yesterday. I said that the 6th Corps -- if the 6th Corps had planned this operation, I would have known about it. I would have been part of it. That is why I can say with certainty that the 6th Corps did not in fact plan this operation. As to whether it was involved to some extent in the implementation itself or in any stage of the operation, I can't say based on what Mr. Fazlic told me about it, whether the 6th Corps was involved to any degree at any stage. But it certainly did not independently and totally on its own plan this operation because this is definitely something I would have known about without a shadow of a doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tirak. Now, you were also asked in cross-examination about the map that's just behind you there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you this: Does the fact that Mr. Delic's name and signature on the top left-hand corner of the map, which you then said indicates he was a commander, does that fact in itself preclude another commander giving orders on the ground in the theatre of operations?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the signature on the map does not automatically preclude the possibility that someone else actually ran the operation on the ground pursuant to his orders or for some other reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view as a military person, is an operation -- well, is a combat operation better run by a command near the theatre of operation or outside of the theatre of operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's a very broad, hypothetical question of no value to this Tribunal, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I wonder this issue was raised during the cross-examination or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It wasn't, Your Honour. I sort of started with a more general objection, but, yes, I agree it wasn't as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I would submit that it does out of cross-examination simply because counsel has put questions to the witness about the map, and from that -- from those questions has elicited answers with respect to who was the commander of the operation. And In doing that, counsel has also relied on the military experience of the witness, which in a sense is what the Prosecution seeks to undertake at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The principle of the redirect examination is to give you an opportunity to question whatever is mentioned and used in the cross-examination, but you cannot broaden the scope of that. Otherwise, we'll sit until midnight. So would you please withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'll withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, counsel for the Defence in cross-examination asked questions about orders and implementation of those orders by commanders, and your evidence, if I can sum up, was that even though orders are given, that doesn't necessarily mean they are implemented or obeyed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as Chief of Staff, did you ever issue orders, whether verbally or in written form, to your subordinates with respect to the organisation or logistics, with respect to your function?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that. This doesn't arise outs of cross-examination. That is attempt to effectively bulk up the responsibility of Chiefs of Staff and it clearly does not arise out of cross-examination. So I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But on this very issue, I believe that the Prosecution has the right to make some clarifications on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We also have the same question. If the Prosecution did not ask, maybe we could do that. You may proceed, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tirak, I'll repeat the question. Did you ever issue orders, whether verbally or in written form, to your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said earlier on that I never issued any orders save for one critical instance, for the simple reason that in my capacity as Chief of Staff, I did not have the powers to issue orders unless under exceptionally extraordinary circumstances having previously been explicitly authorised by the commander. Once again, I only issued one order in the four or five months I spent there in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, now I understand that. Maybe my question was not clear enough. I'm not referring to combat orders or orders concerning issues that are beyond your function, but simply orders that may have naturally derived from your function to units under your -- within the 6th Corps. It's those orders that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's got to be clarified because there's evidence about what -- about Chiefs of Staff having a power to issue orders within the staff where they have subordinates and my learned friend really ought to distinguish between that order between subordinates in the staff and the 6th Corps generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever issue orders to subordinates within the staff of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those orders always obeyed?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would happen sometimes that certain staff members failed to obey orders. It didn't happen very often but it was known to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the occasion that those orders were not obeyed, what did you do to ensure that they were obeyed?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this, and I'll say it again. From our present perspective, it may seem neat when you look at orders and various documents. It seems to make perfect sense. The situation at the time, however, was different because some orders could simply not be implemented, if I may put it that way. On the other hand, there were units around that simply failed to sufficiently comply with any orders that were given. It may sound simple now, but back then it was very difficult to prove that certain units had in fact failed to carry out certain orders. It did sometimes happen that I issued certain orders based on whatever information I had, and it turned out later that it could just not be carried out because the situation on the ground did not allow it. You must know that at the time, it was very often the case that certain orders were simply not carried out. It was even more often the case that orders could not be carried out. That's why you should distinguish between these neat documents which seem to create a picture of a reality that was very different from what was the case on the ground back at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, from those orders that could be carried out -- when you issued orders, did you see it as your responsibility to follow up that those orders were implemented, as the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that does not arise out of cross-examination under any view of it, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. That will be out of scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tirak, I just want to ask you, well, hopefully one or two questions about the Igman -- the battle of Igman -- at Igman. Do you remember speaking about that to counsel for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall counsel for the Defence putting to you that the 9th and 10th Brigades were involved in the battle for Igman?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think what I put was that elements of those brigades were used, not that those brigades were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If there's any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, it matters to me, so I make the objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall counsel for the Defence putting to you that elements of the 9th and 10th Brigades were involved in the battle for Igman?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at the conclusion of the battle whether the VRS, the army of Republika Srpska, or the ABiH -- well, let me ask it a different way. Excuse me. Which army, either the VRS or the ABiH, eventually controlled most of Igman?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of that battle, most of Bjelasnica, Igman, and Treskavica was under the control of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's the re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from the Judges? Yes, Judge El Mahdi. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to seek some clarifications. The first clarification has to do with what you said. You said that if ever the 6th Corps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me. No translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the French channel is not in place. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now, Witness?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. So this has to do with a couple of clarifications would like to obtain from you. So I have a few questions. First question is you did confirm that if ever the 6th Corps had itself carried out combat operations or had combat plans, you would have known about them, about it. Can you confirm this? Is this your position?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will confirm this again just to make it crystal clear. If the 6th Corps -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Fine. If you do confirm, I mean, I understood you to say this. So my question does not relate to this. It is based on something else. You also stated that your military training was solely limited to compulsory military service.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And you added that many orders that were submitted to you during the hearing were not known to you. You had not known about them before. So on what basis do you claim that if ever there had been combat plans, you would have been informed. So much so because you said that most of the time you were absent. You were not in Konjic. Most of the time, you were either in Vakuf or in Fojnica, if I understood properly. Therefore, do you maintain what you said? Don't you think that it would have been possible for some plans to be established without you knowing about them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it would have been possible for plans to be made in my absence. That is entirely possible. But when I said I believed that the 6th Corps did not independently and on its own plan this operation, I said this based on my own experience. Both before and after, throughout my time, in fact, with the 6th Corps, there was never an action organised independently by the 6th Corps that I didn't know of. Since I was away at the time, of course -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but if you were absent. Do you rule out the possibility of plans being established, set up whilst you were not there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can't rule out the possibility that these plans can be made quickly. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Fine. Because you also stated that it was a very critical situation, especially so after the HVO attack in the area.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you're asking me whether I said the situation was critical, the answer is yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I'll move on to another subject, namely your meeting with Mr. Fazlic. Following the meeting, you went to see Mr. Delic. Was the idea that -- was any mention made of you talking to Mr. Halilovic or turning to him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't consider that, because Mr. Fazlic told me to go and see Mr. Delic. Had he told me to go and see Mr. Halilovic, I would have done so. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but then Mr. Fazlic was convinced that Mr. Halilovic did not have any say.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer that question. I really have no idea what he meant. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] What about you? I'm asking for your personal view.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to tell you what I think, my assumption is Mr. Fazlic believed that Mr. Delic was in a position to issue a final order, and that was probably why he sent me to Mr. Delic and not to Mr. Halilovic. Mr. Delic was the commander, after all, not Mr. Halilovic. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Therefore, the effective power was vested with Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a commander of the BH army. Of course the power lay with him. To what extent he was in effective control of the situation is not something that I can say. He was at the time the commander of the BH army and the power was vested in him. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Let me move on to my last question. It is in relation to the 9th Brigade. You said that through a friend living in Sarajevo, you'd heard that he once had to do some work, some trench digging. Apart from that one incident, did you ever hear other complaints of the same kind or -- I believe your friend was a professor, a geography professor, if I'm not mistaken. Apart from him, were there other cases?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only complaint that was ever addressed to me personally. Throughout my time in Sarajevo, I heard about others, but this is the only case that concerned me personally. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So he was the only one to ever speak to you about it, but you never heard anything else, you in person, from anybody else?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean whether any other people came to me to complain, the answer is no, they didn't. I was in no position to -- to help them or do anything about it. However, I heard people talk about such things happening, but the only complaint that I received personally was the one from that particular gentleman. And that should not strike anyone as strange, because my position was such that anyone would come complaining to me. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've heard that people had been kidnapped from their flats, that jewellery was stolen. I heard all kinds of stories, but this is the kind of thing that people talked about on a daily basis on the streets of Sarajevo. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So, regarding the 9th Brigade -- that was regarding the 9th Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And you did not hear anything about the 10th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only incident I was told about occurred before the brigades were even set up. I'm talking about the incident at the Novo Sarajevo Staff. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Did the 9th Brigade have any special insignia, how to make the difference between a member of the 9th Brigade, from them from other members of the army?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no official ranks in the BH army at that time, and -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: I'm talking about brigades. How could you see? How could you identify a soldier as being a member of that particular brigade rather than another brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most brigades had inscriptions, shoulder patches, badges, or some marks of distinction above their shirt pockets. Commanders were doing their best to make their -- make their own units distinctive. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] During that time did other brigade members wear insignias?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD TIRAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about the specific period of time for the simple reason that I don't know. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge El Mahdi. Any questions out of the Judge's questions? I see none. At this stage, are there any documents to tender from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: From the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: MFI 294 and MFI 295.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Possibly, Your Honour. I just want to make sure which ones they are. You might identify this, too. I only know one, and that is -- 295 is the signature on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: 294 was the -- an order from Rasim Delic that was the last document from last night which was went to the -- to the 6th Corps on the 2nd of July 1993. The witness didn't remember that specific order. He indicated that they were very busy at that time, and it may well be there wasn't a plan drafted by them in response to Mr. Delic's order that was sent to them. But it was an order from Delic to the 6th Corps that you will recall. So that's why we wanted to submit it. The witness said he -- he himself can't remember it. But obviously it was received there so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to 295, the document with the signature on the basis that the evidence of the witness has been that he could not confirm that this was intact in Fazlic's signature. So on that basis I can't see how the document can assist Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that's the very reason we would like to have it admitted into the evidence. So the document 294 and 295 are admitted into the evidence. It is so decided. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. After we are adjourned, Madam Usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a very pleasant journey back home. Tomorrow morning, we could sit at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any different opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour. There aren't any different opinions. Could I just indicate that from the matters raised in Court by my learned friend Mr. Re concerning the witness Okic, it may be that we're going to have to ask for some slight delays depending on how things are organised and how Your Honours want to proceed. I won't make submissions now. I understood that there was the possibility of going into tomorrow afternoon. I'm not suggesting that that should or should not be done, but if it has to be done the Defence agrees that we will cooperate and do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And tomorrow morning, at the very beginning I think the Bench would like to hear the parties on their positions concerning the next witness and then we'll consider whether we hear the witness himself or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And how far we could go with that witness. Generally speaking, we would like to divide the testimony of the next witness into two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours. We'll give some thought to what our submissions are about that procedure and what safeguards can be put in place and so on. Your Honours, there's just one other matter, that the issue of the deposition of Vehbija Karic will need to be the subject of submissions tomorrow morning as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid we -- well, you may resume tomorrow morning and I believe that we have already looked into it since it was already brought to our attention last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- having said that, the hearing for today is adjourned. I apologise to the interpreters and all the staff working for these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
